title: You're in Control
tagline: Your character stops doing its own thing and starts doing what you tell it.
newIdea: Input -- the program reacting to you
goals: Use `followMouse()` to make your character chase the cursor
Use `keyboardControl()` to drive your character with the arrow keys
Explain the difference between **continuous** input and an **event**
Use `mousePressed()` to make something happen once per click

vocab.def: information coming into the program from you -- the mouse, the keyboard
a function Processing calls automatically when something happens once, like a click or a key press
runs once, each time you click the mouse
runs when a key is pressed; holding a key may trigger repeated calls
something checked every single frame, inside `draw()` -- like "where is the mouse right now?"

warmup: What does `move()` do, and where does it go?  What happens if you leave it out?

howItWorks.h: Two very different kinds of input
p: This is the real idea of the lesson, and it is worth slowing down for.
Some questions have an answer **all the time**:  "where is the mouse right now?"  You can ask that on every frame.  That is **continuous** input, and it belongs in `draw()`.
A key press is an **event**.  Processing calls `keyPressed()` when it receives that event.  Holding a key may generate repeated key-press events.
`followMouse()` pulls your character toward the cursor a little bit, every frame.  So it goes **inside `draw()`**.

code.label: Following the mouse

bullets: **You must set a velocity first.**  `followMouse()` uses the size of your velocity as its chase speed.  If the velocity is zero, your character will not move an inch and it will look broken.
When you use `followMouse()`, do **not** also call `move()`.  `followMouse()` moves the position itself.  Calling both fights over the same character.

p: `keyboardControl()` reads the arrow keys and sets your character's velocity to match.  It goes **inside `keyPressed()`**, not `draw()`.
This makes a key press change the velocity.  Then `move()` in `draw()` applies that velocity each frame.

code.label: Arrow-key control

howItWorks.h: Your character coasts, and that is not a bug
p: Press an arrow key and let go.  Your character keeps going.
That is correct.  `keyboardControl()` **sets** the velocity, and nothing ever un-sets it.  Releasing the key does not tell the character to stop -- nobody asked it to.
It feels like ice skating.  Some games want exactly that.  If yours does not, that is a great thing to fix later.
`mousePressed()` is another event function.  Whatever you put inside it happens exactly once, each time you click.

code.label: Snap to the mouse on click

steps: Open your Lesson 3 sketch.  The `MyCharacter` tab still does not change.
**Try Option A first.**  In `draw()`, replace `player.move();` with `player.followMouse();`
Make sure `player.setVelocity(4, 0);` is still in `setup()`.  Without it, nothing will move.
Press **▶ Run** and move your mouse around.  Your character should chase the cursor.
Change the `4` in `setVelocity` to `1`, then to `12`.  Slow and stalky, or fast and twitchy?
**Now try Option B.**  Comment out the `followMouse()` line and put `player.move();` back.
Add a `keyPressed()` function at the bottom of your sketch with `player.keyboardControl();` inside it.
Run it.  **Click inside the sketch window first** -- the keyboard is ignored until the window has focus.  Now use the arrow keys.
Press an arrow and let go.  Notice it keeps going.  That is the coasting.
Pick the control style you want to use for the rest of the unit, and delete or comment out the other one.

code.label: Main sketch tab

makeItYours: Try **both** control modes, then pick the one you want for the rest of the unit.
If you chose `followMouse()`:  tune the speed in `setVelocity()` until the chase feels right.
Add a second, non-player blob that moves on its own (copy the pattern from Lesson 3) so the screen is not empty.
If you chose `keyboardControl()`:  add a `mousePressed()` that does something fun -- try `player.moveTo(mouseX, mouseY);` to teleport.
Combine them:  arrow keys to drive, plus a click ability.
challenge: Make the character stop when you release the key.  Add a `keyReleased()` function with `player.setVelocity(0, 0);` inside it.  Now compare the two feels -- which one suits your character?
flintHint: Good things to ask:  "my character will not follow the mouse", "why do the arrow keys do nothing?", or "how do I make my character stop when I let go of the key?"  Tell it which control style you picked.
wrapup: What does `keyboardControl()` change when a key is pressed, and what does `move()` do each frame?
assignmentTask: Take control of your character.  Try both styles, then commit to one and tune it until it feels good.
assignmentDo: Get **both** control styles working, at least briefly.  You need to feel the difference to choose well.
Pick the one that fits the game you want to build, and tune it -- the chase speed, or how it handles the coasting.
Add one extra piece of input if you can:  a `mousePressed()` ability, or a second blob moving on its own.
submit: A short screen recording showing you controlling your character.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Set a speed so `followMouse()` actually moves.
Explain how a key press changes velocity and `move()` applies it each frame.
Tell the difference between continuous input and an event.
standard: Control the character with `followMouse()` or `keyboardControl()`, and distinguish continuous input from event input.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: My character does not respond to input yet.  **Next step:**  for `followMouse`, set a speed with `setVelocity()` in `setup()` -- it needs a speed above 0 to move at all.  For keys, make sure `keyboardControl()` is inside `keyPressed()`, not `draw()`, and that you clicked inside the sketch window first.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: I can drive my character with the mouse or the arrow keys.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I picked the control style that fits my game and tuned it -- a speed that feels right, or a `mousePressed()` that does something fun.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I combined inputs (keyboard control **plus** a `mousePressed()` ability), or added a second blob that moves on its own while I steer the player.

thinking: In one or two sentences:  which control style did you choose for your game, and what made it the right fit?

p: It goes **inside `draw()`** and runs every frame, pulling the character toward the cursor.

It uses `vel.mag()` as the chase speed.  If the velocity is `(0, 0)`, `followMouse()` moves the character exactly zero pixels and looks completely broken.  Call `player.setVelocity(4, 0)` in `setup()`.
Also:  when using `followMouse()`, do **not** call `move()`.  `followMouse()` writes the position directly, and calling both makes the motion fight itself.
It goes **inside `keyPressed()`**.  Not `draw()`.

`keyboardControl()` reads `keyCode` and sets velocity.  Calling it in `draw()` reapplies that setting each frame and can overwrite other velocity changes.  Use `keyPressed()` here so velocity changes in response to a key event.
After `keyPressed()` sets the velocity, `move()` in `draw()` applies it each frame.  So the `draw()` loop still looks exactly like Lesson 3.
This is the transferable idea in the lesson, and it is worth more than either method.
"Where is the mouse?" always has an answer, so you can ask every frame.  "Did the player just press a key?" only has an answer at one instant, so the system has to come tell you.
Frame it as a question they could answer about any program.  It's bigger than these two functions.
Put `followMouse()` in `draw()` and run -- instant, obvious.  Then comment it out, uncomment `move()`, add `keyPressed()`, and run again.
Doing both on the projector in ninety seconds makes the choice concrete before you ask them to pick one.
With `keyboardControl()`, releasing the key leaves the velocity unchanged, so the character coasts.  Students expect it to stop.
This is a genuinely good discussion about **state**:  the character is not "being pushed," it *has* a velocity, and nothing has changed it back.  Nobody told it to stop.
If they want it to stop, `keyReleased()` with `setVelocity(0, 0)` does it.  Offer it only if they ask.

guided: Everyone opens Lesson 3's sketch.  Confirm `setVelocity()` is in `setup()`.
Swap `move()` for `followMouse()` together.  Run.  Everyone chases the cursor for a minute -- let them play, it is fun and it costs nothing.
As a class, change the speed to `1`, then to `12`.  Ask which feels better and why.  There is no right answer; the point is that they have an opinion.
Switch to Option B together:  comment out `followMouse()`, restore `move()`, add `keyPressed()` at the bottom.
**Remind everyone to click inside the sketch window** before using the keyboard.  This will strand people otherwise.
Have everyone press an arrow and release.  Ask what happened.  Run the coasting discussion here.
Students choose their control style and tune it.  Circulate.
pitfalls: **`followMouse()` with no velocity set.**  Moves zero pixels.  Looks broken, is not.  Check `setup()` first every time.
**Calling both `followMouse()` and `move()`.**  The motion fights itself and looks jittery.
**`keyboardControl()` inside `draw()`.**  It reapplies velocity each frame and can overwrite a stop set in `keyReleased()`.  Keep it in `keyPressed()` for this lesson's event-driven pattern.
**Window not focused.**  Keyboard input goes nowhere until they click inside the sketch window.  Costs students five minutes each if you do not warn them.
Deleting `move()` when switching to keyboard control.  The velocity gets set and then never applied.
Expecting the character to stop on key release.  It coasts.  That is state at work, and the code is doing exactly what it was told.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: `keyboardControl()` sets velocity from the key code; `move()` applies that velocity each frame.  Releasing a key leaves velocity unchanged in this starter.  Holding a key may generate repeated `keyPressed()` calls.
notes: Have students try **both** styles before choosing.  The choice is more meaningful if they have felt the alternative, and it is their first real design decision in the unit.
`followMouse()` is easier and more forgiving; `keyboardControl()` feels more like a real game.  Both are fine choices for Lesson 9.
Fast finishers:  `keyReleased()` with `setVelocity(0, 0)`, or a `mousePressed()` ability.  Both are one-liners with a big feel change.
Whatever they choose today, they can change later.  Say that out loud so nobody agonizes.
